summary: Introduces magnetic fields: sources (permanent magnets, currents, moving charges, changing E-fields), visualization via field lines (out of N, into S, closed loops, never cross, density shows strength), the field of a current-carrying wire via the right-hand grip rule, and the Lorentz force on a moving charge F = q(v x B), including the zero-force parallel case and the circular-path perpendicular case.
title: Magnetic Fields

topicTitle: 12.2 Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
summary: Explains why a current-carrying wire in an external magnetic field feels a force (field interaction pushes it from stronger to weaker field region), states F = BIL sin(theta) and the vector form F = I(L x B), covers the maximum (perpendicular, F=BIL) and minimum (parallel, F=0) cases, and gives Fleming's Left-Hand Rule for the force direction.
title: 12.4 Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

summary: Defines magnetic flux density B = F/(IL), gives its SI unit Tesla (and CGS Gauss, 1 T = 10^4 G), explains that B is a vector (magnitude = field strength, direction from field lines), and derives its dimensions [MT^-2 A^-1].
title: Magnetic Flux Density

topicTitle: 12.4 Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
summary: Defines the magnetic force on a moving charge F = q(v x B), covers when it is zero (charge at rest or velocity parallel to B) and why it never does work (always perpendicular to velocity), gives the right-hand rule for direction, explains the resulting circular or helical motion, and surveys applications like cyclotrons and auroras.
title: 12.6 Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

topicTitle: 12.5 Motion of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Magnetic Field
summary: Derives circular motion of a charge in a uniform field by equating magnetic force to centripetal force, giving radius r = mv/(qB), angular frequency omega = qB/m, period T = 2*pi*m/(qB), and cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2*pi*m) (all independent of speed), notes the constant kinetic energy, covers the helical case when velocity has a parallel component, and works a numeric proton-orbit example.
title: Motion of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Magnetic Field

summary: Explains the velocity selector: perpendicular (crossed) E and B fields filter charged particles so only those with v = E/B pass through undeflected (from the Lorentz force F = qE + q(v x B), setting qE = qvB), a result independent of charge and mass, and its use as the first stage of a mass spectrometer.
title: Velocity Selector

summary: Surveys three magnetic field patterns from current geometry: a long straight wire (B = mu0*I/(2*pi*r), concentric circles), a flat circular coil (B = mu0*N*I/(2r) at the center), and a solenoid (B = mu0*n*I inside, uniform like a bar magnet), each with its right-hand-rule direction.
title: Magnetic Field of Electric Currents

summary: Defines a solenoid as a tightly wound coil producing a strong uniform interior field B = mu0*n*I (like a bar magnet), gives the right-hand grip rule for polarity, explains how a ferromagnetic core (electromagnet) amplifies the field via domain alignment and relative permeability (B = mu_r*mu0*n*I), and compares soft iron (switchable) vs steel (retains magnetism) as core materials.
title: 12.7 Magnetic Field in a Solenoid

summary: Explains that parallel currents in the same direction attract while opposite (anti-parallel) currents repel, derives the force per unit length F/L = mu0*I1*I2/(2*pi*r) from combining a single wire's field with F=BIL, confirms the Newton's-third-law action-reaction pairing, and uses this force to define the Ampere as the SI base unit of current.
title: Magnetic Force Between Current-Carrying Conductors

summary: Defines magnetic flux as the total field passing through an area, gives Phi = B.A = BA*cos(theta), its SI unit Weber, covers special cases (maximum when perpendicular, zero when parallel), non-uniform-field flux via integration, and defines magnetic flux density B = Phi/A (Wb/m^2 = Tesla).
title: Magnetic Flux

summary: Defines magnetic flux linkage as the flux through a single turn times the number of turns N (Phi_N = N*B*A*cos(theta)), gives its unit (Weber-turns), distinguishes it from plain magnetic flux, and works numeric examples for coils.
title: Magnetic Flux Linkage

summary: States Faraday's Law e = -N*(delta Phi/delta t), covers the Lenz's-law negative sign, Faraday's moving-magnet and transformer-effect experiments, and the factors affecting induced EMF magnitude (turns, rate of flux change via speed, field strength, and coil area).
title: 12.10 Faraday's Law

summary: States Lenz's Law (the induced current's direction always opposes the change in flux that produced it), ties it to the negative sign in Faraday's Law and to conservation of energy, works a moving-magnet example, and gives Fleming's Right-Hand Rule for finding the induced current direction.
title: 12.11 Lenz's Law

summary: Explains an electromagnetic seismometer as a device that detects seismic waves using Faraday's law: ground shaking moves the frame while a suspended magnet/coil lags due to inertia, inducing a current proportional to ground velocity, plus its advantages over purely mechanical designs.
title: 12.12 Seismometer
